lines.text: A land where rivers meet and empires clashed, of medieval kings, long Ottoman rule, risings and wars. This is the story of Serbia.
Some ten thousand years ago, people settled on the banks of the Danube at Lepenski Vir, one of the oldest villages in Europe.
Where the Sava meets the Danube, a settlement grew that would become Belgrade, a city fought over in more than a hundred wars.
In the twelfth century the Nemanjic family rose to power, and for two hundred years they built a medieval Serbian state.
One of their sons, a monk named Sava, became the first archbishop of the Serbian church, and its most loved saint.
Around 1190 the dynasty raised Studenica, the largest and richest of the medieval Serbian monasteries.
In 1217 Serbia was crowned a kingdom, the beginning of the country whose story runs to this day.
In the next century came Stefan Dusan, a ruler of great ambition, who gave his lands a written code of law.
In 1346 he was crowned tsar, and for a brief time Serbia was an empire, stretching across much of the Balkans.
But the Ottomans were coming. In 1389 the two sides met at Kosovo, a battle Serbs have remembered in song and story ever since.
Centuries of Ottoman rule followed. Then, in 1768, Karadjordje was born, the man who would lead the Serbs to rise.
In 1804 the rising began. After years of fighting, Serbia won the right to rule itself.
In 1856 Nikola Tesla was born to a Serbian family in what is now Croatia. His alternating current would power the world.
Two years later came Mihajlo Pupin, another Serb who made his name as a physicist and inventor in America.
Ivo Andric would write The Bridge on the Drina, and win the Nobel Prize for literature in 1961.
In June 1914, Gavrilo Princip shot the Austrian heir in Sarajevo. Within weeks Europe was at war, and Serbia was its first target.
The cost was terrible. Serbia lost about a sixth of its people in the First World War.
When the war ended in 1918, Serbs joined other South Slavs in one state. Later, under Tito, it became socialist Yugoslavia.
Slobodan Milosevic would rise to lead Serbia as Yugoslavia fell apart in the wars of the nineties.
Aleksandar Vucic, born in 1970, would become president in 2017.
And in Belgrade, Novak Djokovic was born. He would win more men's Grand Slam titles than anyone in history.
In 1995, in neighbouring Bosnia, Bosnian Serb forces killed about eight thousand Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica, a genocide.
Three years later war came to Kosovo itself.
In 1999 NATO bombed Yugoslavia for weeks, until Serbian forces withdrew from Kosovo.
In October 2000, huge crowds filled Belgrade, and Milosevic's rule came to an end.
In 2008 Kosovo declared its independence. Serbia has never recognised it.
In November 2024 the concrete canopy of Novi Sad's station fell, killing sixteen people and setting off months of protest.
From Lepenski Vir to the streets of Novi Sad, Serbia's long story is still unfolding.
